CA-01.001: a collection has zero members if it is empty. to count a finite collection, choose its members and pair each with exactly one number in a counting sequence beginning at one. the last number used tells how many members there are. counting the same members in a different order gives the same result. two collections have equal quantity when each member of one can be paired with a unique member of the other and all members are paired. a group of three stones and a group of three marks have equal counts even though their members differ. the quantity depends on what was selected as a member. grouping pairs of stones as single items changes the question being counted. numeral forms and reading directions are conventions. cardinality numeral
CA-01.002: addition can describe joining collections with no shared members. joining a pair of marks and three more marks gives five: 2 + 3 = 5. equality says that both sides represent the same value. removing a group of three from the five leaves two: 5 − 3 = 2. multiplication can count equally sized groups: three groups of four objects contain twelve objects. dividing twelve into groups of four gives three groups. dividing five whole objects into two equally sized groups leaves one object over if the objects are kept whole. these examples use whole objects. fractions and negative numbers extend the operations to other cases. division by zero has no defined value in ordinary arithmetic. equality remainder
CA-01.003: geometry describes positions, shapes and their relationships. when two straight directions meet, an angle describes their separation. comparing two lengths by division gives a ratio. an object that is twice as long as another has the same length ratio whether the lengths are measured in small or large units. to label positions on a flat surface, choose an origin and two perpendicular axes. in a common convention, two numbers say how far to move along the first and second axes from the origin, using the stated units and directions. changing the origin changes the numbers used for a point. the grid is a flat mathematical model. human orientation conventions and coordinate labels must be established before using a diagram to give directions. origin angle
CA-01.004: binary notation uses two symbols, written as 0 and 1 in this archive. in common positional binary the places have weights one, two, four, eight and onward from right to left. the sequence 101 therefore represents one group of four, no groups of two, and one more, a total of five. two distinguishable states can represent the symbols, as with holes and unmarked positions on a punched card. the record needs a convention for where to start, which direction to read, how to group positions and whether a group encodes a number, a character or a measurement. the meaning of a bit sequence depends on the surrounding agreement about its boundaries and mapping. a photographed ibm card has its own historical code, while the centauri raster uses other rules. bit positional notation
CA-01.005: a ratio compares quantities by division. the ratio 2 to 3 is equal to 4 to 6 because both quantities increased by the same factor. if both quantities are lengths, convert them to the same unit before comparing them. a rate such as distance traveled per time compares different kinds of quantities and carries units. a proportion states that two ratios are equal. if a drawing uses one length unit to represent five of the same unit on an object, a feature three units long in the drawing represents fifteen units. this calculation relies on the same scale factor being used for every length in the comparison. a projection of a large curved surface onto a flat map can vary in scale. the scale of a lens image can also depend on the depth of the object. ratio scale factor
CA-01.006: an exponent shows repeated multiplication when it is a positive whole number. in base ten, ten to the third power is 10 × 10 × 10, or one thousand. a negative integer exponent gives a reciprocal. ten to the power of minus three is one thousandth. scientific notation can express a value as a number with magnitude at least one and less than ten multiplied by a power of ten. for example, 3,200 may be written as 3.2 × 10³. multiplying a quantity by ten changes it by one order of magnitude. comparing widely different scales becomes easier when both are expressed in the same units. writing a value with a power of ten does not make a measurement more accurate. units, significant figures and uncertainty describe different aspects of the measurement. exponent order of magnitude
